messages.body_plain:
I'd like to fit a model that assumes a lognormal distribution.  However, when I specify `family=lognormal()`, I get additive effects on the log scale (which is the reasonable thing in most cases) but I need additive effects on the original scale (which in my case happens to be milliseconds).  Is there a way to achieve this with brms?  For context, see here: http://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/lognormal-with-additive-effects-on-the-original-scale/1776

Thank you,

  Titus

messages.body_plain:
You want to do something like

y ~ lognormal(log(mu + X * a), sigma)

right? You can do this in brms using its non-linear syntax:

fit <- brm(bf(y ~ log(eta), eta ~ <predictors>, nl = TRUE),
           data = <data>, family = lognormal(),
           prior = prior(normal(0, 100), nlpar = eta))

However, I am not sure, if I want to recommend this model. Especially, you need "eta" to be positive, which is not trivial to achieve depending on your predictors.

Perhaps you could try the skew_normal() or exgaussian() families to deal with right-skewed data but handle predictors on the original scale.

messages.body_plain:
Hi BRMS users and developers!

I've built a model in BRMS to represent a meta-analysis with a number of moderators.  It looks like this:

yi | se(sei) ~ pub_year * mod_1 * mod_2 + (1 | id)

I would like to predict the i+1th study based on draws from the posterior distribution.  Is this possible using BRMS?  I thought it would be a matter of using predict() -  for example - I tried following the manual example:

newdata <- data.frame(pub_year = c(2017, 2018),
                      mod_1 = c(0, 1),
                      mod_2 = c(0,1)
                      )
predict(fit, newdata = newdata)

but I get this error:
"Error: The following variables are missing in 'data': 'sei'"

The the sei is unknown so I'm not sure what to enter - does anyone have any clues at all?

Many thanks in advance!

Oliver

messages.subject: priors for bernoulli model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,
 I've been using default priors for my current models. The default is a student_T(3, 0, 10) on the intercept.

 However, I was wondering if I should provide more informative priors. The "prior" information for the disease I'm studying is that it has a prevalence of 0.001 to 0.003 depending on the studied population. In my dataset the prevalence is about 10 times higher, but still, it's only around 0.02 to 0.05.

 So it seems I could constrain the model to a more realistic prior probability range - for instance a prior prevalence between 0 and 0.05 or 0 and 0.1 would be more realistic than 0 to 1.

 It may not matter since I have a lot of observations (nearly 20,000), but it's probably at least worth testing. How would you recommend changing the prior to account for this more realistic prior information?

Thanks,
Paul

Here's an example of a model with a few covariates -

Family: bernoulli(logit)
Formula: Result ~ s(long, lat) + race + CMV_neg + CMV_pos

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] priors for bernoulli model
messages.body_plain:
The Intercept has an improper flat prior over the reals by default.

The student_t(3, 0, 10) prior you mention refers to the standard deviation parameter of the s(long, lat) spline.

Also, you have to keep in mind that all the coefficients are on the logit scale, so it is actually more complicated to reformulate your knowledge about the prevalance into a prior for the Intercept.

A prevalance of 2% would translate to a value of roughly -3.9 on the logit scale, so maybe one could use this information in the prior by using a normal prior centered around -3.9 for the Intercept.

However, I don't think it will change the posterior by much as long as you don't make the prior too narrow, which you probably don't want to do anyway.

Best,
Paul

messages.subject_clean: Constrained multi response regression using brms?
messages.body_plain:
Dear forum,

I have a designed experiment, where I combine all possible pairs, triplets, an quartets, of seven bacterial strains. Each combination is a separet experiment. After growth and subsequent harvest, the relative composition of strains in each experiment is measure using a dna technique.

The purpose of this experiment is to predict the strain composition of new blends of up to seven strains, and the interaction structure between strains, i.e. If the presence of a strain inhibits or stimulates other strains in a given blend.

My design matrix therefore consist of seven columns and 96 rows, one row for each experiment. Each column represents a strain, and the presence or absence of this strain in the inocolum is decoded as 1 and 0, respectively.

The response matrix also consists of seven columns and 96 rows. Each column in the response matrix represents the relative composition of each strain in the final blend after growth in co-culture.

The response, for each strain is therefore constrianed between zero and one, and the sum of the relative compositions of strains is by definition always one. That is, the responses are strongly correlated.

I can figure out how to fit the response of a single strain in brms using Beta regression, but I cannot figure if its possible to impose the sum to one contstraint between the responses.

Is it possible to constrain the responses between one and zero and at the same time forcing the responses to sum to one using brms?

Any ideas would be highly appreciated.

Regards

/jannik

Hi Diva,

Shouldn't it rather be (1|district)+(1|subdistrict:district)?

messages.subject: spatiotemporal hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
I'm starting to work on a new study where my interest is showing spatial migration of odds over time. Briefly, it's around 30,000 tests with 8000 positives performed on 17,000 patients, and I have coordinate pairs for all of them.

Ordinarily if the temporal component weren't included I'd do

 brm( result ~ s( lat , long ) + covariates + ( 1 | ID ), family = "Bernoulli" , data=dat )

In this case I'm adding the random intercept for individual ID to account for individuals who have been tested multiple times (is that the correct syntax and rationale btw?)

However for this project I suspect that the odds of result will migrate over the lat/long field, so I want to put in some sort of temporal hierarchical structure. I can't, however, really consider this like a longitudinal study where the same subjects are tested repeatedly - my lat / long structure is really a whole random field and not individual units like counties that have repeated count data.

I have actual dates of tests, but could I put in a term like ( 1 | month / year ) or ( 1 | month / quarter / year ) for temporal nesting? Do I need to change the correlation structure for the model? Can I then predict odds vs lat/long for each of these time slices and show an animation of how odds temporally migrate over space?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Paul, since you seem surprised of the time it takes, I assume that all the other models were much faster(?)

The "problem" is likely the 3 dimensional spline, which could be too complicated for your data (depending on the distribution of the points in the 3D space). But we will only see this once the model is fitted.

You may try to replace s(...) by t2(...). Sometimes, this will consierably improve sampling speed.

Also, you don't want to use future=TRUE and cores > 1 at the same time. Essentially, when future =TRUE, cores will be ignored, since cores uses the built in parallel stuff of rstan, which is not called when future=TRUE (you will recieve a warning tell you this after having fitted the model).

So unless you want to use futures for some specific reason, just don't use the future argument at all and just go for cores = 4.

Best,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to compare two non-linear models of hyperbolic-discounting that I fit with brms.  The basic question is to test whether different treatments cause subjects to behave differently (as in the full model) or whether there is just a population scaling effect (e.g. the whole population shifts between treatments) but individual subjects use essentially the same strategy in different treatments.

"Full" Model:

full_model = bf(choice ~ inv_logit((rewmag/(1 + exp(logk)*delay) - smag)/noise),
                  noise ~ (1|subjid), logk ~ (treat|subjid), nl = TRUE)

full_fit = brm(full_model,
             data = all_trials, family = bernoulli(link='identity'),
             prior = c(prior(normal(-3,4), nlpar = 'logk'), prior(normal(1,10),lb = 0, nlpar = 'noise')),
             inits = "0",
             chains = 10, iter = 10000, warmup=2000, cores = 10)

"Simpler" Model

simple_model = bf(choice ~ inv_logit((rewmag/(1 + exp(logk)*delay) - smag)/noise),
 noise ~ (1|subjid), logk ~ (1|treat) + (1|subjid), nl = TRUE)

simple_fit = brm(simple_model,
 data = all_trials, family = bernoulli(link='identity'),
 prior = c(prior(normal(-3,4), nlpar = 'logk'), prior(normal(1,10),lb = 0, nlpar = 'noise')),
 inits = "0",
 chains = 20, iter = 25000, warmup=10000, cores = 22)

Both models ran with OK diagnostics (reasonable number of effective samples, Rhat ~ 1).

However, when I run `loo` to do model comparison I get this:

> loo::loo(extract_log_lik(simple_fit$fit, parameter_name = 'lp__')) . # is the lp__ the right thing to use here?
Computed from 200000 by 1 log-likelihood matrix

          Estimate SE
elpd_loo -13748.1 NA
p_loo        91.9 NA
looic     27496.3 NA

Pareto k diagnostic values:
 Count Pct
(-Inf, 0.5] (good) 0 0.0%
 (0.5, 0.7] (ok) 0 0.0%
 (0.7, 1] (bad) 0 0.0%
 (1, Inf) (very bad) 1 100.0%
See help('pareto-k-diagnostic') for details.
Warning message:
Some Pareto k diagnostic values are too high. See help('pareto-k-diagnostic') for details.

Why is the SE==NA?
What does it mean that the Pareto k diagnostic values are too bad. How can I compare the models?

I tried to read Vehtari, et al (2016) but it is over my head.  (Apologies if this would be better asked in a different group).
